questions.q: What guarantee does std::atomic<long>::fetch_add(1) provide that a plain `x = x + 1` on a shared long does not?
options: It guarantees the read, add, and write happen as a single indivisible step no other thread can observe half-finished
It guarantees the value will never exceed INT_MAX
It automatically logs every update for debugging
It converts the variable to a floating-point type
questions.explain: fetch_add performs the read-modify-write atomically, so no other thread can interleave in the middle of the operation — eliminating the race from the plain, non-atomic increment.

questions.q: What happens when compare_exchange_weak fails because another thread already changed the value?
options: It throws a C++ exception
It returns false and writes the actual current value into the 'expected' argument, so the caller can retry
It silently writes the new value anyway
It blocks until the mutex is released
questions.explain: On failure, compare_exchange_weak returns false and updates 'expected' with the atomic's actual current value, which is exactly what a retry loop needs to try again correctly.

questions.q: When is std::memory_order_relaxed an appropriate choice?
options: Whenever you want the strongest ordering guarantee available
Only when working with std::mutex instead of std::atomic
When you only need the atomicity guarantee itself and don't need to order the operation relative to other memory, such as an independent counter
Never — relaxed ordering is always a bug
questions.explain: Relaxed ordering provides atomicity with no additional ordering constraints, which is sufficient and fastest for cases like a statistics counter where only the final total matters.

questions.q: In the latest-price example, why does the publisher use memory_order_release on the 'ready' flag rather than relaxed?
options: Release has no effect and is purely stylistic
Release guarantees that the earlier store to the price variable is visible to any thread that performs a matching acquire load and observes the flag as true
Release makes the store run on a separate thread automatically
Release is required syntactically whenever std::atomic<bool> is used
questions.explain: A release store publishes all writes that happened before it in program order; a matching acquire load that observes the release's effect is guaranteed to see those earlier writes too.

questions.q: What is the default memory ordering used when you call an atomic operation without specifying one explicitly, and why is it a reasonable default?
options: memory_order_relaxed, because it's the fastest
memory_order_seq_cst, because it gives a single global order all threads agree on and is the easiest to reason about correctly
memory_order_acquire, because all reads need it
There is no default — an ordering argument is mandatory
questions.explain: std::memory_order_seq_cst is the default and the strongest ordering; every thread observes atomic operations in one consistent global order, which is the safest starting point before optimizing to a weaker ordering.
